title: Tools for Thought: The History and Future of Mind-Expanding Technology
author: Howard Rheingold
note: Selected: information architect Jorge Arango praises its account of computing as intellectual augmentation; Goodreads 4.10/123 supports positive but modest reader reception. General computing history, not programming instruction. Institutional funding and interface development have worldwide consequences, so neither thematic deduction applies. Forecasts are explicitly historical and reconsidered in the 2000 afterword, not presented as current fact. No serious veto established.
notes: Interview-based history with documented sources; future-facing sections require historical framing.
Links mathematical ideas, hardware, interface design, research funding and intellectual work.
Useful account of how research organizations support tools whose value is not immediately commercial.
Explains development choices and human-computer interaction more fully than circuit mechanisms.

D=8, moderate confidence from Arango's detailed review, contents and reader reports. Successive computing generations add distinct capabilities and constraints; speculative final profiles are less durable. No full-text audit.
Historical explanation remains useful; predictions should not guide present purchasing or technical choices.
Direct fit to computing, technological leverage and scientific organization.
Experienced technology observer with access to central participants; practitioner review supports value.
Profiles provide an accessible sequence of technical changes.
Clear explanatory prose, with occasional visionary rhetoric.

title: Hello World: Being Human in the Age of Algorithms
author: Hannah Fry
note: Selected: Royal Society science-book shortlist, favorable Physics World review by Anna Demming and Goodreads 4.11/12,240. Broad adult explanation of algorithmic decisions, not a technical curriculum. Computing and its deployment dominate; medicine, policing and art are applications, not grounds for thematic deductions. Demming's criticism of low density and limited attention to successes is retained. No serious veto established: the book also compares machine faults with human faults rather than demanding technological rejection.
notes: Concrete applications and explicit limits support the account; dramatic failure examples are not a representative performance survey.
Connects models, data, institutions, incentives and human responsibility across applications.
Useful questions about objectives, error costs, oversight and delegation.
Explains mechanisms at a general-reader level; limited mathematical or implementation depth.

D=6.5, moderate confidence from Demming's review, contrasting reader reports and inspected definition/conclusion passages. Cases introduce different decision failures, but extended anecdotes and basic explanations reduce yield for an expert reader.
Decision principles last; individual algorithm examples date quickly.
Computing, modeling and technological risk fit directly.
Applied mathematician with recognized science-communication work and specialist review attention.
Clear case-based structure builds toward human-machine cooperation.
Readable and controlled, though simplified for broad readership.
referenceEdition: Norton text containing hardcover and paperback ISBNs; alignment unconfirmed

title: Data and Goliath: The Hidden Battles to Collect Your Data and Control Your World
author: Bruce Schneier
note: Selected: strong security-specialist recommendation by Richard Austin in IEEE Cipher and Paul Baccas in Virus Bulletin; Goodreads 4.00/3,902. Criticism is material and retained: Steven Aftergood identifies an omitted favorable assessment of Section 702 and overbroad surveillance language; an ALA journal review finds the treatment one-sided. These lower evidence confidence and score, but do not establish with high confidence that the central account of data collection depends on those claims. Policy reform is not itself partisan recruitment or ideological extremism. General explanation, not specialist training. American policy focus warrants T11; surveillance power and policy dominate T12.
notes: Extensive documentation supports collection practices, but security-benefit counterevidence and distinctions between kinds of surveillance receive uneven treatment.
Connects technical collection, commercial incentives, state surveillance, security and institutions.
Useful principles for data retention, incentives, oversight and privacy-respecting system design.
Explains how collection and reuse scale, with less formal analysis of intervention effects.

D=7.5, moderate confidence from Austin, Baccas, Murdoch and Aftergood. Examples add different data flows and abuses; Murdoch finds the anecdote lists tiring. Detailed proposals add learning beyond repeating the diagnosis.
Core incentive and privacy issues endure; 2015 legal and technical details need historical framing.
Direct relevance to computing, infrastructure and strategic risk.
Security practitioner with substantial technical standing and favorable security-specialist reception.
Three-part progression from mechanisms to consequences to proposals is clear.
Accessible distinctions, weakened by some broad labels and emphatic framing.
